modules.title: Country & Cultural Dimensions Overview
modules.author: Caroline Auer
learning_objectives: Interpret India's six Hofstede scores and their engineering-team implications
Distinguish between national cultural tendencies and individual behavior
Predict which Hofstede dimensions will surface first in a U.S.–India engineering project
modules.drive_scenario: Your company is opening an engineering center in Pune. Week 1: you email your Indian counterpart asking for a direct 'yes or no' on a spec change. No reply for three days.
knowledge_topics: India macro context: fifth-largest economy, 3.1M engineering grads/year, 100+ unicorns
Six Hofstede dimensions with engineering-specific interpretations
High PDI (77): hierarchy, deference, top-down decisions
Moderate collectivism (IDV 48): in-group loyalty, collective credit
Moderate masculinity (MAS 56): achievement-oriented but welfare matters
Low UAI (40): ambiguity tolerance, Jugaad improvisation culture
Long-term orientation (LTO 51): balanced tradition/pragmatism
Restraint (IVR 26): controlled gratification, work-first norms
modules.strategy_framework: High-PDI pre-meeting checklist: Who are the decision-makers? Have senior sponsors been briefed privately first? Is silence from a subordinate agreement or avoidance?

action_items.do: Address senior engineers by title (Dr./Mr./Ms.) until invited otherwise
action_items.avoid: First-name-only email introductions without relationship groundwork
action_items.reason: PDI 77 — titles signal respect and position you as a serious counterpart

action_items.do: Copy the most senior person on emails, even informational ones
action_items.avoid: Flat org chart assumptions — skipping hierarchy in communications
action_items.reason: Hierarchy drives information flow; exclusion can stall projects

action_items.do: Build relationship before agenda — open meetings with personal check-ins
action_items.avoid: Starting with the deliverable and skipping rapport
action_items.reason: Trust precedes commitment in collectivist, high-PDI cultures

branching_scenario.setup: Your Indian team lead goes quiet after you send a design-review request. What do you do?

decision_points.choice_A: Send a follow-up escalating to your manager
decision_points.feedback_A: Incorrect. Escalating before relationship-building signals distrust and may embarrass the lead. (Hofstede et al., 2010; AtoZ International Business, n.d.)
decision_points.choice_B: Schedule a brief call to ask if the design creates any concerns
decision_points.feedback_B: Correct. Indirect check-in preserves face and opens dialogue. High PDI cultures often communicate disagreement indirectly. (Juhász, 2014)

knowledge_checks.question: India's PDI score of 77 most directly predicts which behavior?

options.A: Team members openly challenge manager decisions
options.B: Decisions require senior sign-off before the team acts
options.C: Individual performance reviews are preferred over team reviews
options.D: Engineers change jobs frequently seeking personal advancement

modules.reflection_prompt: Think of a past project where hierarchy or authority affected how decisions were made. How might India's PDI of 77 have changed how you communicated?
modules.primary_interaction: Hofstede explorer — click each dimension to see the score, the engineering-team implication, and an example scenario

modules.title: Business & Engineering Culture
modules.author: Aureo Zanon
learning_objectives: Identify cultural patterns that shape outsourcing and cross-team relationships
Apply boundary-object strategies to close U.S.–India coordination gaps
Use Meyer's culture-map framework to plan a cross-cultural team interaction
modules.drive_scenario: Six months into a U.S.–India outsourcing engagement, you discover the Indian team built a module to a spec you thought you'd updated. The documentation was complete on your end. What went wrong?
knowledge_topics: Outsourcing culture: communication distance, risk tolerance, documentation expectations (Heeks et al., 2001)
Boundary-object creation: joint documentation, overlap hours, joint prototyping (Krishna et al., 2004)
Meyer's Culture Map applied to India: direct vs. indirect feedback, hierarchical vs. egalitarian
Relationship-driven vs. task-driven business culture
In-group vs. out-group dynamics in Indian teams (House et al., 2014)
Psychological safety in hierarchical organizations (Gupta, 2020)
modules.strategy_framework: Meyer's three-step change approach: (1) pre-brief the senior lead privately, (2) reframe in locally meaningful terms, (3) identify and empower a trusted internal champion (Meyer, 2014)

action_items.do: Create joint boundary objects (shared glossary, joint sign-off checklist, overlap-hour meeting)
action_items.avoid: Sending final specs without synchronous confirmation
action_items.reason: Documentation misalignment is a known outsourcing risk (Heeks et al., 2001; Krishna et al., 2004)

action_items.do: Give feedback privately to the team lead first, never in public group settings
action_items.avoid: Raising concerns in a full project call before the lead has heard them
action_items.reason: High PDI + collectivism makes public correction a face-threatening act

action_items.do: Invest in relationship-building before accountability conversations
action_items.avoid: Jumping to metrics and deadlines in first interactions
action_items.reason: Trust precedes commitment; relationships are the contract in India-based partnerships

branching_scenario.setup: Your Indian partner team has missed a deliverable. The client is asking for answers. How do you proceed?

decision_points.choice_A: Email the full team asking for a status update
decision_points.feedback_A: Risk: Group visibility without prior private conversation creates face-threat. (Meyer, 2014)

decision_points.choice_B: Call the team lead privately to understand blockers before any escalation
decision_points.feedback_B: Best practice: private first, then reframe to client. Preserves relationship and opens problem-solving. (Krishna et al., 2004)

modules.primary_interaction: Outsourcing-relationship scenario — step through three real coordination moments and choose the culturally effective path at each

modules.title: Leadership Culture
modules.author: Wenkai Hu
learning_objectives: Compare culturally endorsed vs. observed leadership behaviors using GLOBE data for India
Identify leadership styles that build trust with Indian engineering teams
Apply an ethics lens to a cross-cultural leadership vignette
modules.drive_scenario: You are promoted to lead a mixed U.S.–India team. At your first team meeting you announce a rotating decision-making model so everyone can lead a sprint. Silence follows. Why?
knowledge_topics: GLOBE framework: culturally endorsed implicit leadership theories (CLTs) vs. observed behaviors
India GLOBE profile: humane-oriented and participative (endorsed) vs. self-protective (observed toward out-groups)
In-group/out-group boundary: leadership behaviors differ sharply inside vs. outside trusted circles
Ethics vignette from slide 17: engineering leadership decision under pressure
modules.strategy_framework: GLOBE pre-interaction checklist: (1) Am I inside or outside this team's in-group? (2) Which leadership dimension — humane-oriented, participative, or self-protective — is this person likely performing right now? (3) How do I move from out-group to in-group status?

action_items.do: Show humane orientation first: ask about workload, family milestones, personal goals
action_items.avoid: Leading with authority or formal process before relationship is established
action_items.reason: Humane orientation is the highest-endorsed leadership dimension in India (House et al., 2014)

action_items.do: Introduce egalitarian structures gradually, starting within a trusted sub-team
action_items.avoid: Announcing flat or rotating leadership to a full hierarchy without prior buy-in
action_items.reason: High PDI makes sudden role reversal socially disorienting, not empowering

modules.primary_interaction: GLOBE comparison table: for each leadership dimension, see India's culturally endorsed score vs. observed score, and an engineering-context example

modules.title: Self-Reflection
modules.author: Caroline Auer, Wenkai Hu, Rickey Patel, Christopher Toevs, Aureo Zanon
learning_objectives: Examine your own cultural defaults and how they differ from Indian engineering norms
Build a personal 'my defaults vs. India's expectations' comparison table
Identify your highest-leverage CQ growth area before an India assignment
modules.drive_scenario: Before you land, you have one week to prepare. What cultural assumptions are you bringing that could backfire on Day 1?
knowledge_topics: Team self-reflections as worked examples: five different U.S.-trained engineers examining their own CQ profile
CQ assessment: Drive, Knowledge, Strategy, Action subscales
Common U.S. engineer defaults: direct feedback, flat hierarchy assumptions, task-first culture, individual attribution
modules.strategy_framework: Defaults-gap table: list your default behavior → the Indian expectation → the adjustment you will make
modules.primary_interaction: Team self-reflections (5 worked examples), then learner builds their own 'my defaults vs. India's expectations' table with save-to-localStorage

modules.title: Ethical Awareness in Agricultural Equipment Manufacturing
modules.author: Christopher Toevs
learning_objectives: Apply NSPE, IEI, and OECD ethical frameworks to a cross-cultural engineering decision
Identify ethical risks specific to manufacturing and technology transfer in India
Make and defend an authorization decision using a structured ethics test
modules.drive_scenario: You are the lead engineer on an agricultural equipment line being introduced to rural India. A supplier shortcut saves ₹2,000 per unit. Your local distributor says it's 'standard practice.' You have a shipment decision to make by end of week.
knowledge_topics: NSPE six fundamental canons: public safety paramount, honest practice, sustainability
IEI charter: Indian professional engineering ethics — public safety, honest practice
OECD guidelines: due diligence, labor rights, anti-corruption for MNEs in developing markets
Ethics in rural India context: operator literacy, infrastructure variability, maintenance access
Ethical risks: supplier selection, operator instructions, safe use across literacy levels
modules.strategy_framework: Three-part ethics test: (1) Does this action pass NSPE's public-safety canon? (2) Does it meet IEI's local obligations? (3) Does it comply with OECD due-diligence standards?

action_items.do: Require multilingual safety labels and pictogram-based operator instructions
action_items.avoid: Assuming English instructions are sufficient for rural Indian operators
action_items.reason: NSPE canon 1 + IEI charter: public safety paramount across literacy and language contexts

action_items.do: Document and escalate any supplier deviation from safety specifications
action_items.avoid: Accepting verbal 'standard practice' assurances as due diligence
action_items.reason: OECD due-diligence obligation requires documented evidence of safety compliance

branching_scenario.setup: Would you authorize shipment of the equipment with the supplier's shortcut?

decision_points.choice: Authorize shipment — cost savings are significant and distributor confirms acceptability
decision_points.feedback: Incorrect. Distributor acceptance does not substitute for NSPE/IEI/OECD due diligence. If a failure injures operators, the engineering team bears liability.

decision_points.choice: Hold shipment and require documented safety re-test
decision_points.feedback: Correct. NSPE canon 1 (public safety paramount) + OECD due diligence require engineering-led verification, not distributor assurance. (National Society of Professional Engineers, 2019; OECD, 2023)

decision_points.choice: Authorize with a written caveat in the project file
decision_points.feedback: Insufficient. A paper trail without remediation does not satisfy the safety canon — it documents a known risk you chose not to mitigate.

modules.primary_interaction: 'Would you authorize shipment?' — full branching ethics case covering supplier selection, operator instructions, and safe use

modules.title: Motivation Techniques
modules.author: Wenkai Hu
learning_objectives: Apply Herzberg's two-factor theory in India's high-PDI context
Design a culturally appropriate motivation plan for a named Indian team member
Identify three Monday-morning actions an engineering leader can take immediately
modules.drive_scenario: Your top Indian engineer, Priya, is being recruited away. HR says the counter-offer is a 15% salary bump. You know from the literature that salary ranks lower for Indian IT engineers than in Western samples. What do you offer instead?
knowledge_topics: Herzberg's two-factor theory: motivators (recognition, growth) vs. hygiene (salary, job security)
India-specific motivators: supervisor recognition and job security rank highest (Joseph et al., 2025)
Salary ranks lower than in Western samples for Indian IT engineers (Joseph et al., 2025)
Wellbeing tied to managerial support outperforms individual wellness programs (Nimmi & Jakubik, 2023)
Hierarchical cultures and knowledge-sharing inhibition (Gupta, 2020)
Maslow and McClelland applied to India engineering context (Pennsylvania State University, n.d.)
modules.strategy_framework: Build a motivation plan for a named team member: (1) identify their dominant motivation cluster, (2) match to Herzberg motivators specific to India context, (3) define three concrete actions for Monday

action_items.do: Publicly recognize contributions to senior leadership — name the engineer and the achievement in management meetings
action_items.avoid: Generic team-wide praise that doesn't name individual contributions
action_items.reason: Supervisor recognition is the top retention driver in Indian IT (Joseph et al., 2025)

action_items.do: Invest in formal learning opportunities and certifications tied to their career path
action_items.avoid: Generic 'keep up the good work' without visible career investment
action_items.reason: Growth motivators sustain engagement when hygiene factors (salary) are already adequate

action_items.do: Build managerial support structures — regular 1:1s, clear path to promotion
action_items.avoid: Individually-targeted wellness perks as a retention substitute for managerial presence
action_items.reason: Managerial support outperforms individual programs in Indian IT (Nimmi & Jakubik, 2023)

modules.primary_interaction: 'Three actions an engineering leader can use Monday' — build-your-own motivation plan for a named Indian team member (interactive worksheet, saved to localStorage)

modules.title: Innovation & Diffusion of Innovations
modules.author: Rickey Patel
learning_objectives: Apply Rogers' adopter-category framework to a technology rollout in India
Explain why India's cultural paradox (high PDI + low UAI) shapes the diffusion curve
Design a 'Champions, Not Campaigns' rollout strategy for an India-based team
Identify the accelerators and inhibitors most likely to affect your project
modules.drive_scenario: Your company wants to roll out a new IoT-enabled quality-control system across three Indian manufacturing plants. Your change-management playbook is built for U.S. middle managers. What needs to change?
knowledge_topics: Rogers' five adopter categories with India-specific context (Rogers, 2003)
16% tipping point: once early adopters (13.5%) + innovators (2.5%) adopt, the early majority follows
India's cultural paradox: low UAI (40) enables individual risk-taking BUT high PDI (77) concentrates adoption decisions at authority nodes (Desmarchelier & Fang, 2016)
UPI case study: 0.92B → 131.1B transactions FY2018–FY2024, government mandate as champion (NPCI, 2024; Nilekani & Shah, 2015)
Accelerators: Jugaad innovation culture (Radjou et al., 2012), 3.1M engineering grads/year, government mandates (Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile), ISRO/Chandrayaan-3 credibility effect

Inhibitors: high-PDI authority gating suppresses upward voice (Pavitra & Sarikwal, 2023), regulatory risk (Kearney 2026 FDI rank 22/25), DPDP Act compliance uncertainty, infrastructure variability (World Bank, 2022a)
Dearing & Kreuter mistakes: assuming a good idea sells itself, ignoring social system norms, overlooking champions (Dearing & Kreuter, 2010)
Meyer's champion framework applied to India (Meyer, 2014)
ICAR extension model: institutional champions + train-the-trainer for rural diffusion (Indian Council of Agricultural Research, 2018)
Mark interview: internal champions with organizational authority essential to overcoming adoption resistance (Mark, personal communication, November 14, 2026)
modules.strategy_framework: Three-step champion strategy (Meyer, 2014): (1) Pre-brief senior authority privately; (2) Reframe innovation in locally meaningful terms (cost savings, government alignment, career advancement); (3) Identify and empower a trusted internal champion with organizational authority

action_items.do: Find your senior champion before launching — brief them privately, let them announce
action_items.avoid: Broadcast email announcing 'we're rolling out X starting Monday'
action_items.reason: High PDI: authority-gated adoption requires top-down endorsement (Pavitra & Sarikwal, 2023; Meyer, 2014)

action_items.do: Reframe the innovation in terms your Indian team values: job security, national progress, career growth
action_items.avoid: Leading with efficiency gains or cost savings as the primary value proposition
action_items.reason: Locally meaningful framing activates the low-UAI individual adopter while satisfying the high-PDI group norm

action_items.do: Build a pilot with early adopters (innovators + early adopters ~16%), document wins visibly
action_items.avoid: Waiting for full consensus before beginning
action_items.reason: 16% tipping point (Rogers, 2003): reaching early majority requires visible social proof from credible peers

branching_scenario.setup: You're rolling out a new quality system. You have a one-hour kickoff slot. How do you open?

decision_points.choice: Present data on ROI and global benchmarks
decision_points.feedback: Weak in India context. Data alone does not overcome high-PDI authority-gate. (Dearing & Kreuter, 2010)

decision_points.choice: Have the plant director open with their personal endorsement, then you present
decision_points.feedback: Strong. Authority-gated endorsement activates PDI-consistent adoption channel. (Meyer, 2014; Pavitra & Sarikwal, 2023)

decision_points.choice: Open with the UPI success story as a local analog
decision_points.feedback: Good supporting move, but only effective after senior authority has spoken. Use as evidence, not opener.

modules.primary_interaction: Three separate interactions: (1) Interactive Rogers bell curve — drag threshold to see tipping point; (2) UPI growth chart; (3) Accelerators vs. inhibitors drag-and-sort activity; plus 'Champions, Not Campaigns' mistake-spotter; FDI rank strip

capstone_questions.question: Who has the final say when engineers disagree?
Who owns a failure at the interfaces?
